opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting pattern, and it's something you really notice once you've spent time in both worlds. Roughly speaking, the East Coast, and parts of the Midwest too, has historically been the stronghold of what you might call traditional robotics. Think about places like CMU in Pittsburgh, MIT, or the robotics groups around Boston. That culture grew up around control theory, mechanical design, state estimation, planning: very rigorous, model-based approaches where you write down the dynamics, you reason about guarantees, and you build systems that work reliably in the real world. Boston especially has this hardware-heavy ecosystem, with a lot of companies building actual machines.

The West Coast, especially the Bay Area, has leaned much more toward the machine-learning side. Part of that is just proximity to the big AI labs and the tech companies, where the default instinct is: get a lot of data, scale up the model, and let the system learn the behavior instead of hand-engineering it. So a lot of the robot learning work, end-to-end policies, imitation learning from large demonstration datasets, and now these foundation-model-style approaches for robotics, has a very strong center of gravity there. The culture is faster, more empirical, more willing to try something that doesn't have a clean theoretical justification yet and see whether it scales.

I don't want to overstate it, though. It's a tendency, not a hard border. CMU has done enormous amounts of learning work, and plenty of Bay Area groups care deeply about hardware and control. People move back and forth constantly. But the *default worldview* is different. If you ask a traditional roboticist why a robot failed, they'll often look for a modeling error. If you ask an ML person, they'll often say, well, we probably didn't have enough of the right data.

What's exciting right now is that the two sides are converging. The learning people are discovering that hardware, low-level control, and good system design still matter a lot. You can't just learn your way around a bad actuator. And the traditional people are seeing that learned components can handle things like perception and messy contact-rich manipulation in ways that were really hard to model by hand. The most interesting work, I think, is happening in that middle ground, by people who are fluent in both languages.

r001.rationale: The response describes the East Coast as a historical stronghold of traditional robotics and says its culture grew from model-based robotics traditions.

r002.rationale: It says researchers move back and forth between regions, but does not describe a recent professional gravitation toward Silicon Valley regardless of where they are based.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. It's actually quite striking when you look at where these communities are physically located in the US. The traditional robotics world, by which I mean the people who come from control theory, mechanical engineering, planning, SLAM and so on, has very deep roots in places like Pittsburgh with Carnegie Mellon, and in Boston with MIT and the whole ecosystem around Boston Dynamics. These are places where people have been building physical machines for thirty or forty years, and the culture is very much about reliability, safety, and understanding your system from first principles.

The machine-learning side of robotics, especially the recent wave of large models and imitation learning, is much more concentrated on the West Coast, the Bay Area in particular. You have Stanford and Berkeley, you have Google and the people who came out of Google Brain and DeepMind's robotics efforts, you have OpenAI's influence even after they stopped doing hardware, and then a whole wave of startups like Physical Intelligence and others that essentially grew out of that research culture. The mindset there is very different. It's scale first, data first, and a kind of optimism that the same recipe that worked for language and vision will eventually work for manipulation.

So you end up with a split that's partly geographic but really it's cultural and generational. The East Coast and Pittsburgh crowd will say, show me the guarantees, show me this works ten thousand times in a row on a real factory floor. The West Coast crowd will say, you've been working on this for decades and the robots still can't fold laundry, let the data decide.

What I find interesting is that the divide is starting to blur. A lot of the strongest teams right now deliberately mix both. They hire people who know how to build a good hardware platform and tune a controller, and they put them next to people who know how to train a foundation model. Boston Dynamics itself has been moving toward learning-based approaches, and Bay Area companies are quietly hiring a lot of traditional roboticists because they realize data alone doesn't give you a robot that doesn't break. So I'd say the geography still reflects where the two traditions came from, but the best work is increasingly happening at the intersection, and honestly I think that intersection is where the whole field is going to be in a few years.

r001.rationale: The response places traditional robotics in Pittsburgh and Boston and says these communities have been building physical machines for decades, indicating deeper roots from an earlier lineage.

r002.rationale: It describes machine-learning robotics and startups as concentrated in the Bay Area, but does not say researchers and entrepreneurs have recently gravitated toward Silicon Valley regardless of where they are based.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe it as a difference in emphasis rather than a strict geographic divide. On the East Coast, there’s a strong tradition of approaching robotics through dynamics, control, planning, and carefully designed systems. On the West Coast, especially around the Bay Area, there’s more emphasis on machine learning—asking how much of a robot’s behavior can be learned from data rather than explicitly engineered.

Those approaches also lead to different instincts. One starts with understanding the system and building in structure; the other starts with collecting data and seeing what a model can learn. But there’s plenty of overlap, and I think the most productive work brings those instincts together. A robot still has to operate in the physical world, regardless of how it acquired its capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes an East Coast tradition in dynamics, control, planning, and system design, but does not connect that tradition to an early historical lineage.

r002.rationale: The response does not say researchers or entrepreneurs have recently been moving professionally toward Silicon Valley.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a bit of an East Coast–West Coast divide, although it’s not a clean line. On the East Coast, you see more of the traditional robotics approach: modeling, control, planning, and building systems with explicit structure. On the West Coast, especially around the Bay Area, there’s more emphasis on machine learning—learning from data, scaling up training, and seeing how much of the behavior can emerge from that.

But I wouldn’t treat those as two separate camps. The interesting question is where you need the structure that robotics gives you and where learning can replace something that’s difficult to model or engineer by hand.

r001.rationale: The response associates the East Coast with traditional robotics methods, but says nothing about their early historical lineage or deeper roots.

r002.rationale: It describes a West Coast emphasis on machine learning, but does not say robotics researchers or entrepreneurs have recently gravitated toward Silicon Valley.
